title: Hosted API Demo - Chat & Text Generation Basics
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood Hosted API focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, generation params, retries and error handling. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a user-facing analytics assistant; primary concerns: latency, cost, data retention/SOC2. Agreed next steps: send pricing, security pack, quickstart, and schedule a short benchmark run with sample prompts.

transcript: Meeting Header: 2026-08-30 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~45 mins | Attendees: Ava Martinez, Leo Chen, Jin Park — Pioneer Analytics: Sarah Bloom, Ravi Patel, Marta Lopez, Tom Erickson
[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Ava from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Quick intros?
[00:06] Sarah: Hi I'm Sarah, CTO at Pioneer Analytics. We're looking at embedding a chat assistant into our web app and evaluating hosted options.
[00:11] Ravi: Ravi, ML eng — mainly focused on latency and cost per query, also quality of responses for domain-specific prompts.

[00:18] Ava: Great, thanks. I have Leo (SE) on the call to walk through streaming and params and Jin for follow ups. We'll do a short demo, then dig into retry behavior and error handling, and leave time for security questions.
[00:34] Leo: hi all — quick note, feel free to interrupt. I'll show the console and then a small live call via the SDK and streaming response so you can see token-by-token delivery.

[00:42] [00:42] Leo: Opening the console... (mild keyboard noise) — here is the model catalog. For hosted we surface curated open models plus our verified performance profiles. You can pick models tuned for latency or quality.
[01:05] Tom: Can you explain streaming vs non-streaming in practice? Our web chat needs to feel snappy.

[01:10] Leo: Sure — streaming sends partial tokens as they are generated so the UI can render progressively; it reduces perceived latency. Non-streaming waits for the full response. For low-latency user experiences we recommend streaming with small chunk sizes and a short initial token flush.
[01:26] Ravi: Does streaming change cost?

[01:29] Leo: Not directly — cost is per token generated. But perceived latency improvements can let you tune max_tokens, stopping criteria, or use shorter prompts which reduce cost. Also we support prefix caching and KV cache for repeated context which can drop token counts significantly.
[01:44] Ava: Quick product note — the SDK has helpers for stream parsing and reconnection logic; the REST endpoint also supports chunked transfer encoding for streaming responses.

[02:00] [02:00] Leo: Live demo via JS SDK: demo prompt — "Summarize this user's support ticket and suggest next steps." (typing) — initiating streaming call... (audio: slight pause) — you see tokens coming in, the UI updates progressively.
[02:20] Sarah: Nice — I see partial sentences. What about final ordering or hallucination controls?

[02:25] Leo: We recommend a few levers: temperature (0-1), top_p, and repetition_penalty. For deterministic outputs use temp 0-0.2 and top_p 0.8-1. Also you can use system prompts and few-shot examples to constrain style. We also have our Optimize toolkit that recommends parameter profiles per workload.
[02:44] Ravi: Any defaults you recommend for a QA assistant?
[02:48] Leo: For factual QA: temperature 0.0-0.2, max_tokens tuned to expected answer length, and use stop sequences. For creative tasks higher temp. We can share a param matrix.
[03:05] Tom: How do retries work? We have occasional 5xxs in other providers and want idempotent behavior.

[03:09] Leo: Good question — our client library exposes an idempotency key header. For transient 5xx/429 we do an exponential backoff with jitter; streaming calls we recommend a reconnection strategy that resumes from the last token via an opaque continuation token with compatible model versions. We also surface retry metrics in the console.
[03:29] Sarah: Do you do automatic model fallback if a model is overloaded?

[03:33] Ava: Yes — smart routing can failover to a compatible model variant (slightly lower quality/higher latency tradeoffs) based on policy you define: latency SLO first, or cost-first. For enterprise customers you can pin a model to avoid fallbacks.
[03:50] Marta: Data retention and logs — we need audit trails and to ensure PII isn't retained beyond X days.

[03:55] Ava: Understood — our hosted plan has configurable data retention; we keep request/response logs for the retention window and you can opt out or route to private deployments. We are SOC2 Type 2 certified — I'll send the security pack. We also integrate with customer KMS for key management on Private deployments.
[04:20] Ravi: Any TL;DR on rate limits and quotas? We expect bursts during reports publication.

[04:24] Leo: Hosted has per-account rate limits and token quotas. For bursty workloads we offer burst capacity and we can size commits for Dedicated. On hosted you can request higher quotas; adaptive batching helps smoother throughput.

[04:41] [04:41] Leo: Quick look at request parameters in the console: model, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, streaming flag, and an optional idempotency key. There's also a client-side SDK param for reconnect attempts and backoff.
[04:59] Sarah: Do you support function/tool calling or structured output?

[05:03] Leo: Yes — we support function-like tool calling via JSON schema enforcement; the runtime can return structured payloads and the SDK includes validators to parse it. That helps reduce hallucination for data extraction tasks.
[05:20] Tom: For our analytics assistant, many prompts include user data — do you do token redaction or PII detection automatically?

[05:25] Ava: We provide plugins and integration patterns: you can pre-process inputs to redact or hash PII; we also offer an optional PII-scan pipeline in the Professional/Enterprise tiers that flags sensitive content before logging.
[05:40] Ravi: About latency — what numbers should we expect for a 200 token response on hosted?

[05:44] Leo: It depends on model choice. Our smaller curated models often return 200 tokens in ~150-300ms per chunk (per token latency lower than big models). End-to-end (including network) for a 200-token reply typically ranges 400ms-1.2s for optimized models. We provide per-route latency dashboards so you can set SLOs.
[06:10] Sarah: Cost modelling — do you have per-token pricing and a way to project costs?

[06:14] Ava: Yes, hosted is usage-based per token. Console shows token breakdown by prompt vs completion tokens and the Optimize toolkit recommends quantization/model variants and caching to lower cost. We'll send a cost projection template.

[06:30] [06:30] Leo: Now quick demo of retries: I'll simulate a 429 and show client backoff. (typing noise) — the SDK retries automatically, picks up where it left off for streaming using the continuation token; you see minimal duplication in the UI.
[06:48] Marta: Is the continuation token exposed to customers or handled server-side?
[06:52] Leo: It's handled by the SDK as an opaque token but you can opt to manage reconnections yourself if you want; we document the protocol.
[07:05] Ravi: For production, we'd probably want a small queue in front to smooth bursts. Any recommended architecture?

[07:10] Ava: Common pattern: a small ingress queue + short-lived workers that call Redwood with batching enabled (we provide guidance). For user-facing low-latency, prefer direct streaming from client with edge caching for repeated prefixes.
[07:25] Tom: Can you show the logs/tracing?

[07:28] Leo: Sure — console trace view shows token-level timings, request id, model variant, and retry events. You can filter by route, token cost, or error code. (small pause) — here's an example trace with a fallback event to a cheaper model.
[07:50] Sarah: If we do a pilot, what's the typical timeline?

[07:54] Ava: Pilot can be quick — onboarding + credentials + sample benchmark within 1-2 weeks. If you want SLA-backed Dedicated or Private it'll add provisioning time. For hosted pilot we often do a 2-4 week bench and then decide on commit sizing.
[08:10] Ravi: Are there any gotchas for streaming over flaky mobile networks?
[08:14] Leo: Reconnect/resume is the strategy. For mobile we recommend shorter initial responses and progressive hydration. Also use client-side caching for repeated contextual prompts.
[08:28] Marta: Security doc and SOC2 please — send to our security contact (marta@pioneer.ai).
[08:32] Ava: Will do. I'll include the SOC2 report, data retention options, and our security whitepaper.
[08:40] [08:40] Leo: One last note — you can set per-route parameter presets so different UI flows use a different temperature/max_tokens without code changes.
[08:52] Tom: Good to know. Any limitations around max request size?

[08:55] Leo: There's a context length limit per model (e.g., 8k, 32k variants). For large contexts we suggest retrieval-augmented generation with a vector DB and retrieval snippets to keep prompt size reasonable.
[09:10] Sarah: Alright let's recap and agree next steps.

[09:13] Ava: Recap: demo of streaming and SDK, discussed params and retries, and security/compliance. Next steps — we'll send pricing, quickstart, security pack, and benchmark harness; you provide prompts and SLOs; schedule a benchmark run mid-September.
[09:29] Sarah: Sounds good. Any quick notes on billing or committed discounts?
[09:33] Ava: For hosted we have usage tiers; committed reserved capacity (Dedicated) offers discounts and predictable throughput. I'll include both options in the pricing doc.
[09:44] Ravi: Thanks — excited to run some tests.
[09:47] Ava: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts and calendar invite for the bench. Bye!
[09:52] Call ended
